vln_trans.title: VLN-Trans: Translator for the Vision and Language Navigation Agent
vln_trans.problem: The task is graph-based R2R/R4R navigation from a full instruction and panoramic observations. The motivating mismatch is specific: an instructor may name a landmark the visual encoder cannot recognize, or name a category shared by multiple candidate views. The output is a next-viewpoint distribution including STOP; the method assumes access to the current candidate views and offline navigation trajectories. It is not an online general-purpose LLM paraphraser.
vln_trans.method:
SyFiS constructs step-level motion-plus-landmark sentences from R2R and PREVALENT trajectories. Relative heading/elevation chooses one of six motion classes; CLIP ranks a fixed label vocabulary, and a target-exclusive recognized label supplies a positive landmark. Irrelevant labels give easy negatives and shared labels give hard negatives (§3.2). This uniqueness is relative to CLIP detections, not a verified property of the scene.

Separate text and visual LSTMs feed cross-modal soft attention. Its hidden vectors provide translated representations. Pretraining combines token-generation CE (SG) with a margin-based triplet objective (DSL). At navigation time an additional MLP predicts per-token relevance weights; the recurrent VLN-BERT text input concatenates original, translated, and relevance-weighted original features (§3.3–3.4, Eqs 4–11). The actual output used by the navigator is latent representation, not a rewritten natural-language string (§6).

Training combines supervised expert action loss and sampled RL, plus SG and sub-instruction-split supervision where aligned FG-R2R/SyFiS data exist. Eq 9 is a schematic and incomplete RL notation; a reward/advantage estimator is needed to operationalize it. Eq 10 prints only a positive BCE term, so released code must establish the actual binary objective. ResNet-152 visual features, BERT language initialization, AdamW, translator batch 16/lr 1e−5 and navigation 300k iterations are specified (§4.2). Navigation pretraining additionally uses RxR and Marky-mT5. Inference is greedy recurrent viewpoint selection. Paper reports approximately two days for base pretraining on four RTX2080s and one day for fine-tuning on one unspecified RTX GPU; these are author timings.
vln_trans.novelty: Relative to Speaker-Follower, the generated supervision is local and discriminative across candidates rather than a whole-route caption. Relative to FG-R2R and ADAPT, SyFiS explicitly chooses a recognizable candidate-exclusive landmark. The online translator is trained latent conditioning, so a frozen-LLM textual rewriting baseline tests a related but different mechanism. Data and architecture must be separated: Table 1 includes base VLN-BERT, added RxR/Marky data, further SyFiS data, and translator variants.
vln_trans.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 1/PDF p7 improves unseen-validation SR from .63 for the original base to .65 with extra data, .67 with SyFiS, and .69 with FG-R2R-trained VLN-Trans. The data-matched ++ baseline has SPL .61 versus .63 for the full method. Test SR is .63 for the ++ baseline versus .66 for the full method. Table 4/p8 gives the more controlled comparison: full alignment objectives reach .690 SR/.633 SPL versus .672/.611 for ++. These support a contribution beyond extra data in that experiment, but not a six-point pure architectural gain.

Table 4 also shows sub-instruction split supervision hurting R2R-Last (.503→.484 SR), where only one instruction sentence exists. R4R Table 2 reports .46 SR/.25 sDTW versus reproduced VLN-BERT .43/.21. Quality assessment uses only 50 generated instructions and yields 58% human success; it is not a guarantee of semantic faithfulness. Figures 4 and 7/p9,13 document wrong landmark associations driven by training frequencies (kitchen–oven/cabinet, hall–pillar). The explicit limitations acknowledge latent interpretability and simulated-only evaluation. Verdict: useful local grounding and supervision, but the translator can substitute a statistically related object without preserving the user’s intended referent.

findings.claim: The online translator contributes latent sub-instruction representations rather than an actual rewritten instruction.
Extra navigation pretraining data already improve the baseline, and Table4 provides a data-matched ++ control.

vln_trans.implementation: INSPECTED CODE: The navigator constructs its translator representation from current candidate/panorama features and original language embeddings, then concatenates the speaker latent and soft-selected instruction representation (r2r_src_navigator/agent.py:310–390,700–746). Supervised sub-instruction and splitting targets enter losses after the representation calculation; this inspected path is not evidence of test-label leakage. The decoder consumes language embeddings directly, not generated text (model.py:207–310). Translator pretraining combines generation cross-entropy with three-negative triplet loss (r2r_src_translator/speaker.py:240–315). This confirms that a textual rewriting control must be separately implemented. The released training launcher specifies PREVALENT, Places365, AdamW, learning rate 1e-5, batch 16, maximum 15 actions and hard-coded author-local augmentation/checkpoint paths. The evaluator uses endpoint success within three metres and shortest-path SPL (eval.py:97–114). README provides processed R2R/R4R, SyFiS, features and checkpoint links, but its train_agent/test_agent launcher names differ from the available train_nav/test_nav names. gela.title: Grounded Entity-Landmark Adaptive Pre-training for Vision-and-Language Navigation
gela.problem: GELA targets the absence of direct phrase-to-landmark supervision in graph VLN. It assumes panoramic RGB features, navigation history, a full instruction/dialogue, and human annotations during training. At inference it predicts next graph node or STOP. Its adaptive pretraining is an offline stage, not test-time adaptation.
gela.method:
GEL-R2R annotates 71,467 entity phrases and 150,183 panoramic landmark boxes over R2R train/validation splits (Table 1). Training uses only the training annotations; the validation annotations support analysis. Annotators follow free-phrase, coreference, alignment, and unique-landmark rules, with expert revision (§3).

The HAMT/LXMERT-derived transformer has text, current 36-view panorama and history encoders, followed by cross-modal attention. Instruction outputs are token vectors Z, view outputs S have 37 entries including STOP, and hidden width is 768. EPP pools marked landmark views and predicts a distribution over the L+1 text positions. LBP pools marked phrase tokens and regresses a normalized 4D box with smooth-L1 plus generalized-IoU loss. ELSA is symmetric multi-positive contrastive alignment over matching visual/text tokens, with temperature .07 (§4.3, Eqs 1–8). The printed pooling products depend on the masks’ normalization; a binary mask would sum rather than average.

Adaptive pretraining retains MLM, MRC, ITM, SAP and spatial-relation proxy tasks to avoid forgetting; augmented data without boxes contribute only those original tasks. New loss weights and box GIoU weight are 1. Pretraining uses 200k iterations, batch 64 per GPU, lr 5e−5, two 3090s. Fine-tuning uses IL plus RL for 100k iterations at 1e−5, batch 16 R2R/batch 8 CVDN (§5.1). R2R experiments separately include no visual augmentation, style transfer, or semantic-mask image synthesis. Inference uses the pretrained navigation transformer without annotation access or an online phrase-grounding oracle.
gela.novelty: The important addition over FG-R2R and Landmark-RxR is entity-to-region human supervision inside sub-instructions, not just temporal sentence-to-subtrajectory alignment. The objectives adapt phrase-grounding ideas from MDETR/TransVG to panoramic HAMT representations. This is a combination of a new annotation resource and grounded auxiliary pretraining; it is not a new large foundation backbone.
gela.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 2/p6 gives no-augmentation HAMT SR 65.7/SPL 60.9 versus GELA 69.2/63.4 on R2R unseen validation. With semantic-mask visual augmentation GELA reaches 71.1/65.0; attributing that whole result to entity alignment alone would conflate augmentation. Table 5/p8 shows EPP alone 65.8 SR and LBP alone 65.6, ELSA 66.3, EPP+LBP 67.0, all three 69.2. This is evidence of complementary objectives; it does not show every auxiliary is individually beneficial. CVDN test goal progress rises 5.58→5.87m (Table 4), a different metric from success.

Figure 3’s effective-attention score increases on annotated pairs. DEDUCTION: an attention-alignment diagnostic does not establish that the correct grounded entity causally determines a navigation action; a controlled landmark intervention would be stronger. Authors acknowledge costly limited annotation (§5.5). Their object-only/scene-only comparison also changes available data volume, explicitly acknowledged, so it cannot cleanly rank semantic category importance. Verdict: a concrete supervision resource and modest controlled gains; robustness under misleading, missing or repeated landmarks is not established.

findings.claim: GELA is offline entity-grounding adaptive pretraining on HAMT, not online test-time adaptation.
EPP and LBP alone do not improve the R2R baseline in Table5, whereas their combination with ELSA does.

navnuances.title: Navigating the Nuances: A Fine-grained Evaluation of Vision-Language Navigation
navnuances.problem: Standard endpoint SR and broad path metrics can hide failures to obey individual direction, ordinal, landmark or region concepts. NavNuances is an evaluation dataset and protocol, not a new trained navigation architecture. Its environment is the static Matterport3D navigation graph, with model-specific input/action interfaces preserved. Some diagnostic scenes overlap environments used by existing training sets; it tests atomic concepts rather than a uniformly unseen-scene generalization protocol.
navnuances.method:
A context-free grammar is iteratively expanded with GPT-4 parsing and manual corrections, then used to construct five categories. Candidate paths come from graph geometry and Habitat semantic annotations; humans reject ambiguous starts and provide/check trajectories; GPT-4 enriches linguistic wording (§3, appendicesD–I). Counts are 579 direction,170 vertical,78 numerical,275 region and 685 landmark instances. There is no new learned loss. NavGPT4v adds directly indexed panoramic images to NavGPT’s text/history prompt.

Metrics differ by category and must not be called ordinary R2R SR. Direction success considers the first movement in a 120-degree left/right/back sector. Moving towards a landmark only requires ending closer to its center; walking past requires a geometric projection on the start–end segment plus final distance within 3m. Numerical success requires both endpoint proximity and nDTW closer to the correct route than competing same-start ordinal routes. Region entry requires stopping inside an adjacent matching region; exit means outside the starting region. Vertical success is endpoint proximity (AppendixB). Dual SR requires both paired left/right commands to succeed from one starting view, directly exposing input insensitivity.

The random baseline takes five graph moves. Two extra ordinal controls know room layout, or layout plus side, but not ordinal semantics. This isolates more of the counting requirement than a uniform random walk. Expensive GPT-4 variants are evaluated on a random subset of roughly 130 examples (§4.3), and prompts supply explicit bearings and candidate IDs. Human and model action interfaces differ, limiting simple architecture attribution.
navnuances.novelty: Relative to general instruction perturbation tests, this contribution uses semantically grounded, category-specific success definitions and paired contrasts. It is direct prior art for left/right counterfactual evaluation and ordinal route discrimination. It does not establish a universal causal measure of language reliance: candidate geometry, visual encoders, pretraining and action interfaces differ across models.
navnuances.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 2/p6 shows DUET R2R SR 71.52 but direction 64.76, numerical 26.92 and landmark 35.76. ScaleVLN raises R2R SR to 80.97 while numerical stays 26.92 and landmark is 29.92. This is a diagnostic association, not proof that synthetic scaling causes instruction neglect: the compared models and training recipes are not a randomized data intervention. NavGPT4v’s subset results are 92.68 direction,39.13 numerical,62.87 landmark,56.25 region and 13.64 vertical; its R2R SR 41.30 illustrates task-specific strengths/tradeoffs.

The ordinal-aware random controls score 32.06 (layout) and 41.03 (layout+side), exceeding several trained agents; this makes their claimed numerical ability weaker than raw SR suggests (§4.4/Fig 4). ScaleVLN’s right-turn SR exceeds left by 18.23 points (§4.4/p9); paired Dual SR exposes selective biases. AppendixC and Figures 13–15 document stopping outside a room and confusing beside with past, including an orientation misreading. These support concrete spatial-predicate failure modes, not universal failure of VLM reasoning.

Limitations explicitly exclude long-instruction error correction and editable-scene counterfactuals. Only 78 numerical examples, including two fifth and two sixth room cases, give weak coverage of high counts. Verdict: an essential diagnostic baseline and source of controlled contrasts; extending it to long-route, off-path states or persistent uncertainty requires additional validated annotations.

findings.claim: NavNuances already uses paired directional commands and Dual SR to diagnose selective bias.
Its numerical criterion compares the executed path against competing same-start ordinal routes using nDTW.

fstta.title: Fast-Slow Test-Time Adaptation for Online Vision-and-Language Navigation
fstta.problem: FSTTA adapts a pretrained navigation policy during a stream of unlabeled test episodes. The policy sees instructions, panoramas, object/history features and a changing candidate graph; no success feedback is required. The targeted tradeoff is rapid per-step adaptation versus accumulation of erroneous updates. It is gradient-based test-time learning, not training-free inference.
fstta.method:
The original policy (principally DUET, also HM3D-scaled variants and continuous baselines) supplies action probabilities. Entropy H(p)=−Σp log p gives a self-supervised loss. Only a small set of late normalization affine parameters is intended to update. Every M steps, centered recent gradients form G∈R^(M×D); covariance eigenvectors define axes, and the mean gradient is reweighted inversely by eigenvalue before length normalization (Eqs 3–5). Gradient-variance departure from a historical EMA scales the learning rate within bounds (Eq 6).

Every N episodes, a slow stage analyzes N+1 parameter snapshots. A recency-weighted displacement from a historical reference supplies a direction; high-variance parameter axes receive more weight, sign-aligned to that displacement (Eqs 8–11). Thus fast and slow stages intentionally favor opposite covariance eigenspaces. Default M=3,N=4, fast/slow rates 6e−4/1e−3 and q=.1 apply to DUET; R2R-CE uses M=7 and different rates. Batch 1 evaluation shuffles each split five times; parameters persist across episodes (§4, AppendixA).

DEDUCTION: centered covariance rank is at most M−1, so for M=3 and D=768 the literal inverse-eigenvalue formula has at least 766 zero eigenvalues. Numerical stabilization is essential, not optional. The released fast helper floors eigenvalues, but its omission of the paper’s norm calibration changes the update magnitude. SVD/PCA requires additional memory and computation; no measured runtime was reproduced.
fstta.novelty: Unlike Tent-style independent entropy steps or resetting at each episode, FSTTA couples recent within-episode gradients and cross-episode parameter trajectories. Its novelty is an optimization schedule and geometric update transformation, not a new semantic navigation model. Later FeedTTA/ATENA add external outcome feedback, changing the information available at deployment.
fstta.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: REVERIE unseen validation DUET SR 46.98/SPL 33.73 becomes 54.15/36.41; test SR 52.51 becomes 53.40 (Table 1). The smaller test gain matters. Ablation Table 2/p7 gives 49.74 SR with fast updates,49.82 with dynamic rate and 54.15 with slow updates. R2R unseen SR 72→75/SPL 60→62 also increases path length 13.94→14.64m (Table 6), consistent with an exploration/efficiency tradeoff. Continuous BEVBert test SR 59→60 while NE worsens 4.70→5.45m (Table 12); gains are not uniform across metrics.

The forgetting test returns to seen validation after adapting on unseen data and retains similar SR (Table 3). This supports retention for that finite sequence, not a guarantee under arbitrary lifelong shifts. Authors explicitly acknowledge shuffled static test episodes as an imperfect online deployment simulation, fixed update frequencies and added cost (§5). Some copied baseline rows violate OSR≥SR (for example DREAMW Table 8), so comparative table transcription needs cross-checking. Verdict: meaningful unlabeled TTA idea with controlled ablations, but confidence optimization can still reinforce a wrong action and the current release has material reproducibility defects.
fstta.implementation:
INSPECTED CODE: Official pinned source is read-only. map_nav_src/models/FSTTA.py implements the active FAST class, covariance eigendecomposition with 1e−6 floor (lines 25–69), entropy backward and update (76–169), and the slow module (254–336). The fast path writes the inverse-covariance direction directly into p.grad at 138 without Eq 5 length calibration. Its entropy helper at 344–346 computes softmax times log_softmax without masking negative infinities; DUET masked logits can therefore require additional numerical handling.

The agent initializes FAST once per rollout (agent_obj.py:374–382), preserving its gradient window within an episode, and maintains SLOW snapshots across episodes (384–408,588–628). However agent_obj.py:37 imports principal_grad from FSTTA.py, and the inspected module defines no such function. The slow PCA helper at 602–609 uses norm/vector rather than vector/norm. These are static release findings, not evidence that published experiments used this exact snapshot. Model/pretrain and graph evaluator paths inherit DUET. feedtta.title: Test-Time Adaptation for Online Vision-Language Navigation with Feedback-based Reinforcement Learning
feedtta.problem: A pretrained VLN policy receives a stream of test tasks and a binary success/failure label after each episode. It must improve future navigation without stepwise expert trajectories. Feedback is an additional supervision source: validation experiments use outcome labels, while the hidden-goal test split uses an LLM oracle. This setting differs fundamentally from unlabeled FSTTA and from frozen-policy zero-shot inference.
feedtta.method:
Terminal feedback F∈{−1,+1} is discounted backward as G_t=γ^(T−t−1)F and multiplies each chosen action’s log-probability gradient (Eqs 1–3). Language/visual encoders are frozen; cross-modal and subsequent policy modules adapt. Batch 1, lr 5e−6, one A100 are reported (§4.3). Stochastic Gradient Reversion (SGR) independently selects gradient coordinates with Bernoulli probability p and multiplies them by negative α, with a scaling correction for other coordinates. It is stochastic optimization noise, not an actual alternate trajectory or causal intervention.

The printed Eq 5 and AppendixB.1 disagree: Eq 5 scales only unselected coordinates by 1/(αp+1−p), while the appendix normalizes the entire modified gradient. The latter is expectation preserving; the literal Eq 5 generally is not. Moreover both negative-α forms have expected absolute multiplier greater than 1 when the denominator is positive. The claimed shrinkage in Eqs 8–9 does not follow. The paper’s approximation assumes |α|<p, whereas REVERIE uses α=−.2 with p=.01/.05. R2R/CE implementation details even list α=+.1, outside the stated negative-reversion mechanism. These are mathematical/reporting limitations, not a refutation of the benchmark results.

The LLM oracle first extracts the goal, then judges a final panorama. AppendixA explicitly permits category substitution and partial alignment, ignoring exact placement. It therefore evaluates broad goal appearance rather than complete route or instance compliance. Adapted Success Rate averages success retention and conversion conditional on the frozen base outcome; it balances the two conditional groups rather than measuring ordinary population success.
feedtta.novelty: Relative to FSTTA, the key change is outcome-conditioned online REINFORCE plus coordinate gradient perturbation. The meaningful experimental comparison needs matched access to binary labels, update parameters and episode order. It is prior art for learning from episodic failure and for using a VLM as a terminal verifier, but its oracle is intentionally lenient about spatial detail.
feedtta.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 1/p6 reports DUET unseen REVERIE SR 46.98→66.49/SPL 33.73→45.38 with outcome feedback, but hidden test SR 52.51→53.58 using the LLM oracle. Table 4/p8 gives GPT-4o feedback accuracy .72, precision .68, and navigation SR 52.29/SPL 33.56: SR improves over base 46.98 but SPL is slightly below base 33.73. Reliable feedback is a major boundary condition. Table 5 separates unregularized feedback RL 63.14 SR from SGR 66.49.

AppendixD shows sequence dependence: randomly interleaved episodes 65.33 SR versus scene-contiguous 54.81, both above 46.98 base but far from invariant behavior. In per-scene case 7 SPL falls 35.21→30.53 despite SR rising. Table 6’s seen-retention result raises SR but lowers SPL 63.94→62.74, so “no forgetting” is metric-specific. Randomly corrupted feedback experiments do not establish robustness to systematic false positives from the lenient LLM prompt. Verdict: strong evidence that extra outcome supervision can improve this stream protocol; mathematical explanations of SGR and claims of broad oracle reliability need correction and controlled verification.
feedtta.implementation: No official FeedTTA implementation was located in the supplied paper, official PMLR page, author-site search, or exact-title/GitHub searches as of the cutoff. The available ATENA repository is a subsequent distinct method and is not relabeled as FeedTTA code. Consequently the SGR implementation variant, REINFORCE sampling/greedy behavior, and exact terminal feedback path cannot be verified here. Reproduction requires these missing details and released policy assets. Only independent scalar checks of the printed mathematics were executed.

atena.title: Active Test-time Vision-Language Navigation
atena.venue: NeurIPS 2025 (volume 38; author repository BibTeX uses 2026 publication year)

sources.locator: Official supplementary appendix,7 PDF pages read

associated: Official supplementary 5981_SUPPLE.pdf, all7 pages read; saved under evidence/04/supplements.
atena.problem: ATENA adapts pretrained navigation policies after episodes while limiting external binary-feedback requests. Its input is a test stream plus occasional outcome labels, and it outputs both a navigation policy update and a predicted success/failure label. Low-entropy episodes use self-predicted labels rather than human labels. It is not a no-training navigation system, and its reported human oracle is simulated from benchmark outcomes in released validation code.
atena.method:
For chosen action a*, form q=λ onehot(a*)+(1−λ)π. Minimize episode-average entropy H(q) for success and maximize it for failure (Eqs 1–4). The one-hot term sharpens the selected action, but its choice is treated as fixed for differentiation. An episode’s average original action entropy selects the feedback source. High entropy requests an external label; low entropy uses sigmoid(fφ(mean_t s_t))>.5. A BCE loss trains this outcome head on either true feedback or its own hard pseudo-label; joint policy/head adaptation occurs after termination (Eqs 5–8).

The source DUET implementation pools concatenated global/local current-state features (width 2×768), computes mixture entropy over nonzero candidates, and uses outcome-dependent sign. Released REVERIE config sets batch 1, λ=.5, threshold .1, external/self learning rates 5e−6/1e−7 and BCE weight .25. AdamW is recreated every episode, so its momentum does not persist. Inference still uses DUET’s graph, including return to the node with best cached STOP score.

SupplementA.7 correctly derives a (1−λ) chain-rule factor but then compares only log-probability gaps when claiming stronger updates. A larger log-ratio gap alone does not imply a larger parameter gradient. At λ→1 the gradient vanishes; isolated binary examples demonstrate nonuniform strength. Entropy also depends on candidate count and is not itself a calibrated success probability. This narrows the mechanism’s interpretation without rejecting its empirical ablations.
atena.novelty: Compared with FeedTTA’s feedback REINFORCE, ATENA uses signed mixture entropy and selective feedback/self-labeling. Compared with ordinary entropy TTA, the binary outcome chooses whether to sharpen or flatten. Generic outcome prediction and uncertainty-based query selection are established components; the contribution is their navigation-specific combination and mixture objective.
atena.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 1/p7 reports DUET unseen REVERIE SR 46.98→68.11/SPL 33.73→45.82, whereas hidden test SR 52.51→54.28. SupplementA.2 says hidden test uses GPT-4o with FeedTTA prompts, changing feedback quality. Table 4 controls feedback access and gives MEO without SAL 63.70 SR versus active Tent 55.69; Table 5 adds SAL to 68.11. SupplementA.4’s outcome-head confusion matrix gives 908 true positives,216 false positives,98 false negatives and 541 true negatives:82.19% accuracy, but positive predictive value is about 80.8%, not 90.26% (the latter is recall).

fgr2r.title: Sub-Instruction Aware Vision-and-Language Navigation
fgr2r.problem: R2R endpoint success can conceal failure to execute intermediate instructions. The paper introduces human sub-instruction–subtrajectory alignment and a recurrent controller that explicitly tracks a single instruction chunk. The environment is the discretized Matterport3D graph; instructions and route segments are assumed to be monotonically ordered.
fgr2r.method: A Stanford dependency-parser heuristic splits instructions at roots, conjunctions, and parataxis, then merges short or action-only fragments (Algorithm 1). The full instruction is encoded by an LSTM before hidden states are partitioned, preserving earlier linguistic context. A chunk-specific attention replaces whole-instruction attention. An LSTM-based shifting head combines the current state, memory, selected-action visual feature, attended chunk, and one-hot count of remaining chunks (Eqs. 4–6). It can advance exactly one chunk and cannot return to an earlier chunk. Action cross-entropy and balanced binary shifting cross-entropy supervise training; student forcing supplies action rollouts while chunk shifts use teacher forcing. Ground-truth shift is positive within 0.5 m of the annotated segment endpoint. The Back-Translation variant applies shifting loss only to its imitation branch. Inference uses predicted shifts and actions. FGR2R adds an average of 3.6 chunks per instruction and 2.4 viewpoints per chunk. Fifty-eight qualified annotators survived a 126-person qualification process. Single-viewpoint chunks are merged during training but retained in validation (Appendix A.1). Models use the original baseline hyperparameters and one Tesla K80.
fgr2r.novelty: Relative to soft whole-instruction attention and progress monitors, the contribution is explicit chunk selection, supervised transitions, and traceable intermediate evaluation. Concurrent BabyWalk uses automatically aligned chunks and curriculum learning, whereas FGR2R uses human alignment. The method is not an instruction-error detector or backward recovery controller.
fgr2r.results: PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 1, PDF p. 7, reports unseen Speaker-Follower SR 29.8→34.7 and nDTW 0.54→0.59; Self-Monitoring SR 40.7→42.4. Back-Translation barely changes, SR 46.6→46.7, while nDTW falls 0.70→0.69. Table 2 shows best shifting F1 only 0.331 and recall 0.209 despite precision 0.806. Thus explicit alignment helps some agents, but correct timing remains weak. Table 3 finds greater endpoint errors for object-specific or condition-dependent chunks; this is descriptive clustering, not a causal isolation of language difficulty. Appendix Table 4 shows R4R Back-Translation SR 31.2→21.5 despite nDTW 0.39→0.48: concatenation leaves bridge viewpoints without instructions and introduces intermediate STOP language. Figure 10 provides a negative case in which perfect chunk shifting still fails object grounding. These results separate progress tracking, grounding, and endpoint success.

Its complete source tree contains the chunker and utilities, not the paper navigator, shift predictor, training objective or evaluator. uln.title: ULN: Towards Underspecified Vision-and-Language Navigation
uln.problem: An agent trained on detailed route instructions often fails when users omit details or provide only a destination. R2R-ULN progressively simplifies existing instructions into L1 (redundancy removed), L2 (partial route), and L3 (goal description). It tests English indoor graph navigation, not arbitrary contradictory instructions.
uln.method: A pooled-word classifier selects low-level versus high-level instruction processing. Granularity Specific Sub-networks (GSS) are identified by transplanting components from a separately trained goal-only agent and measuring validation gain: the recurrent VLN-BERT text encoder or HAMT cross-modal encoder is the selected component. That component is retrained on R2R-last with the remaining agent frozen. At inference an uncertainty MLP consumes visual-to-text attention and action logits. It is trained from randomly dropped training sub-instructions, with teacher-action disagreement as the binary label. Above threshold 0.5, the agent physically explores top candidates and scores current plus future maximum logits (Eq. 7); history state is frozen to delay premature text progression. Reported settings use one-step lookahead, gamma 1.2, and at most three exploration triggers. Training uses original R2R and last sentences, mixed imitation/A2C, AdamW on one GPU: base/classifier 300,000 iterations, selected high-level component 10,000 iterations, uncertainty model 10 epochs. No ULN evaluation instructions are required as training examples, but the architecture-selection protocol measures L3 validation performance and should be separated from held-out testing.
uln.novelty: Combines granularity-specific routing with a learned grounding-error trigger and explicit lookahead. Active VLN instead trains a separate exploration policy using navigation reward; ULN reuses its policy and freezes history. It is prior art for uncertainty-triggered navigation exploration and text-conditioned expert routing, not a zero-training method.

HAMT GSS 43.5/39.5 becomes 44.6/25.9 with E2E and path length 12.91→28.31 m. Table 7 makes the tradeoff explicit: threshold zero can collapse SPL although SR rises. Table 5 does not uniformly support improvement at every level: HAMT L1 SR 56.4→55.5 with full method. Human L3 SR is 75 versus L0 86 (Table 2), so underspecification can also increase human ambiguity. Appendix Table 12 finds adding REVERIE/SOON is not automatically useful. Default evaluation subsamples levels at unequal rates; full-set ablations must not be mixed with Table 4 denominators. The paper establishes useful SR gains, not efficient or calibrated uncertainty resolution.

babywalk.title: BabyWalk: Going Farther in Vision-and-Language Navigation by Taking Baby Steps
babywalk.problem: Policies learned on short route instructions lose fidelity on longer routes. BabyWalk studies transfer across R2R, R4R, and constructed R6R/R8R sequences in the same Matterport3D navigation formalism. Longer tasks are concatenations of R2R routes, not independently authored real-world missions.
babywalk.method: Heuristics extract landmark phrases and chunk instructions into baby steps. A weakly supervised landmark classifier uses trajectory-level object-word labels: state logits are max-pooled and optimized with binary cross-entropy. Dynamic programming chooses monotonically ordered chunk endpoints from average landmark scores (Appendix A). Each chunk has a language LSTM; past chunks and their executed trajectories are separately encoded, exponentially weighted with recency coefficient 0.5, and fused by an MLP. A recurrent cross-modal policy consumes current panorama, prior action, current chunk and remembered context. Imitation learning initially resets the agent to expert chunk-start context; curriculum policy-gradient training then executes increasingly long suffixes of one to four chunks. Terminal reward is SR plus CLS, with zero intermediate reward (Appendix B.2). Inference needs only heuristic chunks and the agent’s own trajectories, not expert alignment. Features are ResNet-152 2048 plus 128-dimensional tiled orientation; hidden size 512, GloVe words 300. Adam learning rate 1e-4, 50,000 imitation iterations then 10,000 per lecture; RL samples eight trajectories per instruction and discounts by 0.95.
babywalk.novelty: The combination of weak automatic chunk alignment, hierarchical recency memory, and length curriculum distinguishes BabyWalk from Speaker-Follower, RCM, and progress-monitor agents. Compared with concurrent FGR2R, supervision is automatically aligned rather than human chunk annotations. Memory forgetting and curriculum should be credited separately from additional speaker augmentation.
babywalk.results: PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 2, PDF p. 7, R4R-trained BabyWalk achieves R4R SR 29.6, CLS 47.8, SDTW 18.1 versus FAST 36.2/34.0/15.5. It prioritizes route fidelity rather than winning endpoint SR. R8R SDTW 11.5 exceeds FAST 6.3, but R8R SR remains 26.3. Table 3, p. 8, removing memory lowers R4R SDTW 17.3→9.9; learned LSTM summary yields 14.4. Table 4 separates curriculum from ordinary RL: SDTW 13.6→17.3 in-domain and 14.1→17.5 on other datasets. Speaker-augmented BabyWalk has lower SR than its unaugmented counterpart in several settings; extra data do not uniformly improve the target metric. The evidence supports hierarchical training for concatenated length transfer, not arbitrary compositional generalization.
babywalk.implementation: INSPECTED CODE: src/follower.py:149–202 reconstructs prior subtask context and combines history embeddings using L1-normalized exponential recency weights, default decay 0.5; negative decay selects learned LSTM memory. This is an explicit forgetting inductive bias, not perfect retention. Sequential inference starts each new subtask at the previous executed endpoint and heading and appends its realized history (486–548). The training driver branches among imitation, reward training and curriculum RL; it advances curriculum and resets optimizers at the configured interval (train_follower.py:50–82,156–194). process_data.py constructs period/landmark chunks and curriculum tasks; no new VLM is involved. Assets and Matterport simulator were not loaded. Inspected source supports the staged mechanism, not independently reproduced long-route scores.

knowno.title: Robots That Ask For Help: Uncertainty Alignment for Large Language Model Planners
knowno.problem: An LLM planner must choose actions under ambiguous language and request human clarification only when necessary. This is manipulation/planning research rather than an R2R route-following method. Context includes already grounded textual observations; the theorem assumes correct low-level execution and accurate human help.
knowno.method: An LLM proposes four candidate actions and an appended other-action option. A second prompt scores the answer letters. Calibration uses nonconformity 1 minus the true-label score and a finite-sample conformal quantile. At inference, labels above the threshold form a prediction set; a singleton is executed, otherwise a human selects a valid option or halts. For a fixed calibration dataset the paper uses a beta-quantile tolerance bound with N=400 and delta=0.01. Multi-step calibration uses the minimum true-label score across an entire correct-action sequence, then constructs per-step sets causally with the same threshold. Appendix A3 handles several acceptable actions by following the highest-scored acceptable branch during both calibration and human-assisted deployment. No model fine-tuning is required; labelled calibration scenarios and human intervention are required. Most experiments use PaLM-2L; ensemble baselines require 20 queries.
knowno.novelty: Extends conformal prediction to language-planning choices and dependent multi-step execution, contrasting prompt-only uncertainty and cumulative-softmax thresholding. Coverage does not require accurate model probabilities; minimal expected set-size claims require the additional assumption that the relevant score models true conditional probabilities. Minimal set size is a different objective from minimizing the probability of requesting help or human response effort.
knowno.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: Hardware Table 1, p. 7, KnowNo plan success 0.76, task success 0.74, per-step help 0.58 versus Simple Set 0.76/0.72/0.72 in 50 trials. Hardware mobile manipulation Table 2, p. 8, plan success 0.87 and physical task success 0.76 with help 0.67; matched-plan-success Simple Set needs help 0.81. The planning versus physical success gap directly demonstrates the limit of the execution assumption. Appendix A4 has only ten bimanual trials. DEDUCTION: the coverage guarantee is distributional, not a guarantee conditional on each particular task or on only the no-help subset. Sequence-level minimum scores are not generally joint sequence probabilities, so do not infer optimal help rate from calibrated step scores. The paper’s own §6 acknowledges grounding/control uncertainty and inaccurate human responses are outside scope.

APPENDIX SCOPE: pp. 17–19 constrain hardware scenarios to avoid visually confusable detections; some challenging mobile tasks use known object locations and scripted execution policies. Figures A9–A11 retain multiple acceptable answers in some scenarios. Calibration concerns the specified scenario/label distribution and successful high-level option selection with the stated help assumptions; it does not independently certify the learned detector or low-level controller.

explore_confident.title: Explore until Confident: Efficient Exploration for Embodied Question Answering
explore_confident.problem: Explore an unknown indoor scene until there is sufficient visual evidence to answer a multiple-choice question. Inputs include RGB-D, camera intrinsics, localization, and a collision-free local planner. Simulation assumes perfect odometry and movements of at most 3 m between queried viewpoints.
explore_confident.method:
Prismatic VLM scores answer options, image-question relevance, and exploration directions marked on the RGB image. Local semantic value normalizes scores among three projected free-space points; global semantic value scores whether any direction is worth exploring. Their exponentially scaled sum is smoothed into a TSDF-derived map and weights frontier sampling. The map is built online from depth. For stopping, rho_t(y)=Rel_t*(p_t(y)-1), and episode score is min_t rho_t(y). A conformal threshold calibrated on full exploration episodes gives per-step answer sets whose running intersection retains the correct answer simultaneously over all prefixes with marginal probability at least 1-epsilon under the same scenario distribution and policy. Stop when the intersection is a singleton. At timeout or an empty intersection, choose the most likely answer at the most relevant view: this fallback is outside the singleton guarantee. Low relevance gives scores near zero, intentionally preventing irrelevant views from removing many answers. The main method has no additional VLM training but uses 300 labelled calibration episodes; an optional separate fine-tuning experiment is reported.

FULL-VERSION APPENDIX CHECK: arXiv v2, PDF p. 15, proves that the trajectory-minimum score exceeds a calibrated threshold exactly when every step retains the true answer in its prediction set. Thus the simultaneous-coverage event carries to any stop within that fixed scenario trajectory, under the scenario exchangeability and calibration assumptions in the main paper. This is an answer-set statement, not a guarantee of collision-free control, accurate localization or finite-time singleton termination. The same appendix uses a cropped explored-view update and frontier weights exp(SV + SV_normal) with a 3 m lookahead along frontier normals. The released repository audit below still did not locate the CP calibration/intersection path.
explore_confident.novelty: Combines visually prompted semantic frontier exploration with sequence-calibrated answer stopping. KnowNo already supplies multi-step conformal calibration; here the set is intersected over repeated observations of a common answer rather than used to request human action labels. This is not a general proof of optimal exploration or conditional accuracy on stopped episodes.
explore_confident.results:
HM-EQA contains 500 GPT-4V-generated, human-filtered questions across 267 HM3D scenes. Exploration comparisons use all 500 at fixed horizons; stopping comparisons split 300 calibration/200 test. Figure 9, p. 10: about 58% answer success requires 71% of the maximum steps versus 85% for a relevance-threshold baseline. Main raw VLM success saturates near 60%; §VII-E reports a separate fine-tuned model 56.2→68.1%. Six hardware scenarios yield four correct answers for this method and relevance baseline; several relevant views still produce wrong answers. These results support efficient exploration and calibrated set retention, not universal high answer accuracy. §VIII acknowledges orientation is omitted from semantic values, single-view reasoning is limited, and prediction sets do not yet guide exploration.

FULL-VERSION APPENDIX CHECK: pp. 16–17 find that extra exploration does not reliably help small-object state questions, and report no gain for identification questions requiring stronger semantic location inference. A view-orientation heuristic raises reported success from 58.4% to 59.3%; replacing the VLM raises it to 65.3% with LLaVA 1.6 or 73.9% with GPT-4V. These are separate component changes, not evidence that the stopping mechanism itself caused all gains.

gsavln.title: General Scene Adaptation for Vision-and-Language Navigation
gsavln.problem: Repeated instructions in a persistent scene permit memory-based adaptation beyond independent-episode VLN. GSA-R2R extends evaluation to 150 residential/non-residential MP3D/HM3D scenes and synthetic Basic, Scene, and User styles. It evaluates within-scene accumulation, not necessarily retention across a continual stream of different domains.
gsavln.method: A speaker generates route instructions, a navigation model identifies failures, GPT-4 refines failed instructions from panoramas/path visualizations, and GPT-4o rewrites styles using building-user roles or character profiles. Six hundred paths per scene are sampled. GR-DUET retains one topological graph across episodes, including node positions and visual observations, while resetting per-episode visited flags. Offline pretraining exposes complete training-scene graphs; fine-tuning accumulates scene-specific graphs and resets them after 50 episodes. PREVALENT augmentation improves path diversity. At test time the proposed method adapts its graph inputs rather than necessarily updating weights. Evaluation uses batch 1, three shuffled instruction sequences, and checkpoint selection by mean validation SPL. The paper reports 180 million parameters, up to 4.3 GB GPU memory, and 67 ms inference excluding feature extraction; those are author measurements on their setup.
gsavln.novelty: The benchmark broadens persistent-scene adaptation to environmental and language-style shifts. GR-DUET preserves graph structure unlike TourHAMT’s long history-token stream and trains for the resulting expanded input. It is a DUET derivative and should be separated from supervised continual learning and feedback-based online parameter updates.

m3e.title: M³E: Continual Vision-and-Language Navigation via Mixture of Macro and Micro Experts
m3e.problem: Replay-free adaptation to sequential scene domains while retaining previous navigation skill. The protocol trains on 80% of each selected val-unseen scene and evaluates held-out episodes and previous domains; this is supervised domain-incremental learning, not unlabeled online TTA.
m3e.method: NaviLLM/Vicuna-based policy encodes 36-view panoramas and instruction/history into a decoder-only LLM. An online cognitive map supplies node features X in R^(N×d); a GNN propagates topology and instruction attention pools a scene vector. A macro MLP routes from this scene vector, while a micro MLP routes each token. Fused expert weights are beta*w_macro+(1-beta)*w_micro with beta=0.3. Six MoE-LoRA experts, top 2 active, rank 16 and scale 32 modify FFN and attention projections. After supervised learning on each new domain, summed routing weights estimate expert workload. Top-K experts receive momentum 0.4 on old parameters; other experts receive 0.6. Consolidation interpolates old and new weights. This statistic measures frequency of use, not a causal contribution to retained task performance. Batch 4, AdamW lr 2e-5, five epochs per domain, A800 80 GB GPUs; no earlier trajectories are replayed.
m3e.novelty: Hierarchical scene/token routing plus expert-dependent consolidation targets continual adaptation on an LLM agent. SAME already uses multimodal state-aware expert routing for joint multi-task training; PerpR/ESR address forgetting with stored trajectories. M3E differs in supervised sequential consolidation without replay, not in inventing MoE or scene memory.

continualvln.title: Continual Vision-and-Language Navigation
continualvln.problem: Sequential scene-domain training causes forgetting. I-CVLN combines English R2R/RxR into 20 domains with over 600 training episodes each; D-CVLN groups CVDN scenes into 11 domains. Evaluation episodes come from the same domains with novel instructions. Domain identity is supplied during training, not inference.
continualvln.method:
Perplexity Replay (PerpR) ranks completed episodes by exp(-mean log probability of agent actions), retains difficult high-perplexity trajectories and removes easy ones from a fixed buffer. Training sums supervised imitation losses on current and replay data. Episodic Self-Replay (ESR) stores previous action-logit sequences and reconstructs the corresponding trajectory with stored decisions, then adds squared logit distillation to current-domain and supervised replay losses; both replay coefficients are 0.2. PerpR and ESR are separate variants, with ESR using random reservoir-style episode selection. I-CVLN uses OSCAR-initialized recurrent VLN-BERT and 500 buffered episodes; D-CVLN uses randomly initialized HAMT and 100 buffered episodes. Three scene-order curricula are averaged. No human clarification policy is learned by D-CVLN: its inputs are recorded dialogue histories.

SUPPLEMENT CHECK: pp. 2–4 specify A3C plus imitation CE, batch eight, 4,000/5,000 iterations per domain on an A100. PerpR sorts new episodes by descending action perplexity and evicts low-perplexity stored episodes under a domain quota. ESR replays the stored logit-argmax action sequence to revisit corresponding states, then distills current versus stored logits while also using ground-truth action labels. The pseudocode shorthand applying a loss to argmax should not be interpreted as a differentiable literal CE formula; the text describes CE supervision.
continualvln.novelty: Adds explicit continual VLN benchmarks and adapts difficulty-based rehearsal and sequential logit distillation to navigation. It differs from IVLN’s within-environment episodic memory: this is parameter learning over scene domains with retained training examples.

Results establish partial forgetting mitigation with a substantial joint-training gap. Table 3 reversing PerpR selection lowers I-CVLN SR 28.9→27.1. Table 4 removing logit replay lowers SR 31.1→24.9 in a single curriculum. Table 2 does not establish strictly monotonic buffer gains: D-CVLN PerpR GP falls 6.2→6.0 from 100 to 200 episodes. Calling vanilla/joint mathematical lower/upper bounds is too strong; they are empirical comparators, and some baselines score below vanilla.

same.title: SAME: Learning Generic Language-Guided Visual Navigation with State-Adaptive Mixture of Experts
same.problem: Naively mixing fine-grained route following, coarse object referring, dialogue and ObjectNav data produces conflicting navigation behavior. SAME aims for one trained policy across tasks, not continual parameter adaptation at inference.
same.method: DUET’s global and local cross-modal encoders are retained. Visual-query projections become sparse MoE layers with eight experts and top-2 routing. Routing input concatenates mean panoramic visual features with language CLS, projects to hidden dimension, and produces expert weights. The mixture output is a weighted sum of selected projections. DAgger supervised action loss is combined with load-balancing loss weighted 0.8. Initialization is ScaleVLN pretraining (4.9 million synthetic examples); fine-tuning samples ScaleVLN:R2R:RxR-EN:CVDN:REVERIE:SOON:Habitat-Web at 10:1:1:1:1:1:2, keeping each batch from one dataset. AdamW lr 1e-5, 20,000 iterations, batch 16, one A100 80 GB. Continuous ObjectNav demonstrations are converted to graph trajectories with endpoint and connectivity filtering; 58,803 remain. Inference uses state-conditioned experts without task identity. Zero-shot CE transfer adds a waypoint predictor, not zero-training end-to-end navigation.
same.novelty: Targets state-varying rather than token-only, task-only, or language-only routing and locates experts in visual query projections. It is a DUET-based multi-dataset method, distinct from VLM policy backbones and from M3E’s sequential expert consolidation.

slow4fast.title: Towards Open Environments and Instructions: General Vision-Language Navigation via Fast-Slow Interactive Reasoning
slow4fast.problem: GSA-R2R agents must reuse experience across episodes and handle scene/user instruction styles. The fast agent is DUET; a Llama3.2-vision slow component summarizes navigation history into reusable experiences.
slow4fast.method: Each step logs viewpoint, topology, instruction, action, visual description and metrics. A CoT prompt turns logs into scene type, spatial context/rules, navigation strategy, historical success rate and frequency. Retrieved experiences are encoded and attended to by visual features: queries are visual features, keys/values are experience vectors. Concatenation and a learned projection fuse attended experience into DUET inputs. An LLM also rewrites styled instructions to Basic style, retaining the original below a confidence threshold. This rewriting occurs during navigation training; the learned fusion is not an entirely training-free method. Library capacity is tuned in the 50–100 range. The main paper delegates exact prompt, retrieval, confidence and training details to supplementary material.
slow4fast.novelty: Adds an LLM-derived experience library and explicit style conversion to GR-DUET-like persistent-scene navigation. GSA-VLN already tested text style translation; this paper’s contribution is the combined experience-to-policy interaction, not the first use of rewriting in this setting.

mind_error.title: Mind the Error! Detection and Localization of Instruction Errors in Vision-and-Language Navigation
mind_error.venue: IROS 2024; official author repository identifies the accepted paper.
mind_error.problem: Detect whether an instruction contains an erroneous direction, room, or object reference, and localize the suspect words after a navigator has executed a trajectory. This is a diagnostic task with a fixed BEVBert navigator, rather than an online language repair policy.
mind_error.method: R2RIE-CE creates paired original/corrupted instructions using direction antonyms and room/object substitutions, with ConceptNet and manual constraints for more plausible replacements. Instruction BERT embeddings use up to 80 tokens of width 768. CLIP visual features from selected trajectory views, positional embeddings, and a CLS token feed four layers of cross-attention with trajectory queries and instruction keys/values, followed by self-attention and feed-forward blocks. Binary error classification uses the CLS output; a separate token head predicts error positions. Training combines binary error cross-entropy and token localization cross-entropy. The 9,000-step AdamW run trains on all error categories without commonsense filtering; the reported checkpoint is selected by validation-unseen AUC on the commonsense all-error set. Inference consumes the completed trajectory, not just the current view.
mind_error.novelty: Introduces instruction-error detection and localization as distinct from instruction underspecification in ULN and language-following diagnostics in NavNuances. It operationalizes instruction/trajectory inconsistency, but does not identify whether an inconsistency was caused by the instruction or by the fixed navigator.
mind_error.results: PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table II reports AUC/average token distance of 0.58/8.13 for directions, 0.80/7.73 for rooms, 0.74/9.21 for objects, 0.91/7.34 for room plus object, and 0.94/6.14 for all errors; mean 0.79/7.71. Object localization is worse than the CLIP baseline token distance 8.76. The large all-error AUC therefore should not be presented as accurate single-word repair or strong directional-error recognition. On natural R2R-CE annotations, 25 of 1,839 instructions are flagged and eight confirmed; on RxR-CE, 118 of 3,669 are flagged and ten confirmed, including mesh-related issues. These selected-case confirmations are not an estimated corpus-wide error rate. The causal ambiguity between language error and policy error remains unresolved.
mind_error.implementation: INSPECTED CODE: The BEV-based trajectory matcher uses a learned trajectory CLS token, positional encoding and crossmodal encoder, with binary detection and an 80-position localization head (vlnce_baselines/models/bev/vilmodel_cmt.py:687–742). ss_trainer_BEV.py:1755–1789 explicitly says navigation imitation loss is not used to fine-tune the navigator in this phase, and combines binary cross-entropy with per-error token cross-entropy. The tokenizer maximum and trajectory representation constrain the scope of localization; this is a trajectory/instruction inconsistency detector, not a causal proof that the language rather than behavior is wrong. README pins Habitat0.1.7 and links model/data resources. Source was inspected, not imported or executed; no detector quality was independently reproduced.

aiuta.title: Collaborative Instance Object Navigation: Leveraging Uncertainty-Awareness to Minimize Human-Agent Dialogues
aiuta.problem: Find a particular object instance in an unknown continuous HM3D scene using an initial object category and dialogue with a user who knows the exact target. The agent does not see the target image; the simulated user does. Multiple same-category distractors make ordinary ObjectNav insufficient.
aiuta.method: AIUTA wraps VLFM frontier navigation, BLIP-2 value mapping, and Grounding DINO detection. At a candidate object, LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B generates a caption and GPT-4o proposes attribute questions. The visual model scores yes/no/unknown and normalized three-way entropy selects uncertain questions with threshold 0.75. Object-presence checks may continue exploration. A language model compares accumulated facts to user answers on a 0–10 scale: high alignment (at least 7) permits stopping, low alignment (below 5) skips the candidate, and intermediate scores trigger more questions. The method allows up to four dialogue rounds and filters uncertain attributes. CoIN contains 1,649 episodes: 831 seen categories, 359 synonyms, 459 unseen categories; at least two distractors, start distance 5–20 m, success within 0.25 m of a goal viewpoint, and 500 actions. The main navigation method uses pretrained models without task fine-tuning, but depends on a truthful target-aware user and tuned decision thresholds.
aiuta.novelty: Adds instance-specific collaborative verification and uncertainty-filtered dialogue to open-vocabulary object navigation. KnowNo calibrates action sets with formal distributional coverage; AIUTA instead uses heuristic entropy and alignment scores. Its user access changes the information available relative to category-only VLFM.

activevig.title: Active Visual Information Gathering for Vision-Language Navigation
activevig.problem: An instruction follower can move briefly to obtain useful visual evidence before committing to its next navigation direction. This requires explicit accounting of exploratory motion, including motion that reveals an already cached view.
activevig.method: An EnvDrop-style LSTM navigator encodes panoramic ResNet-152 and orientation features into 512-dimensional visual tokens and attends to 512-dimensional instruction representations. A nested exploration policy chooses a direction or exploration STOP. An exploration LSTM and knowledge LSTM summarize newly attended neighbors, producing residual updates to candidate-direction features. Multi-step exploration may inspect several directions before the navigator acts. Late action uses cached observations and executes only necessary paths to new views in the static navigation graph. Supervised shortest-path navigation and exploration initialization precede actor-critic training. Navigation rewards use goal-distance progress and terminal rewards; exploration rewards measure change in downstream navigation reward minus a 0.1 step cost. Separate critics are used. Curriculum increases maximum exploration from one to six steps, with four selected; 176,000 speaker-generated examples augment training. Exploration at inference is physical lookahead, not a learned world-model rollout.
activevig.novelty: Learns when and where to gather new visual evidence, rather than only attending to a fixed panorama. It precedes ULN’s uncertainty-triggered physical branches and explicitly includes trajectory cost. Late action is a cache/execution optimization under a static graph, not a simulator-free imagined transition model.

Table 1 test SR increases EnvDrop 0.51→0.60 while SPL falls 0.47→0.41 and TL rises 11.7→21.6. These are reliability/efficiency tradeoffs, not metric-wise dominance. Page 14 reports exploration at 15.3% of navigation steps, correcting 65.2% of initially wrong actions but corrupting 10.7% of initially correct actions. Pre-exploration with synthetic-data fine-tuning and beam search are separate settings: the latter has TL 204.4 and SPL 0.05 despite SR 0.70.

ieve.title: Instance-aware Exploration-Verification-Exploitation for Instance ImageGoal Navigation
ieve.problem: Find the exact object instance shown in a goal image, using RGB-D and pose in an unknown environment. This is Instance ImageGoal Navigation, not language-conditioned route following. Camera height and field of view may differ between goal and current observation.
ieve.method: A classifier identifies the central goal-image object category. RGB-D detections are projected to point clouds, voxelized, pooled, and merged into a 2+N-channel global semantic map. DISK descriptors and LightGlue matching yield instance match count omega. Distance-dependent low/high thresholds select exploration, verification, or exploitation: weak evidence explores; ambiguous evidence approaches for a better view; sufficient matching commits to the candidate; a close poor match rejects it. A learned exploration policy emits a waypoint every ten local steps, with area-coverage and target rewards. FMM generates local motion; low-level actions include continuous linear/angular velocity, camera pitch, and stop, bounded by 35 cm translation and 60 degree rotation per frame. Training uses HM3D scenes and a constructed instance re-identification dataset. Evaluation success requires proximity within one metre and oracle visibility, with 1,000 validation episodes.
ieve.novelty: The explicit approach-to-verify stage adjusts evidence acquisition to distance-dependent instance matching quality. It separates category exploration from instance commitment instead of treating a fixed matching threshold as sufficient at all viewpoints. It does not supply a conformal or probabilistic correctness guarantee.
ieve.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 1 Mod-IIN SR/SPL 0.561/0.233 versus Swin/Mask IEVE 0.684/0.241 and InternImage version 0.702/0.252. Table 2 controlled EVE versus exploration/exploitation improves 0.590/0.221→0.666/0.235 with the same Mask classifier/perception and 0.620/0.216→0.684/0.241 with Swin classification. Oracle classification/segmentation reaches 0.850/0.399, leaving a nonzero planning gap. Classification changes interact with the segmentation backbone, so the full gain cannot be attributed solely to verification. Re-identification experiments show fixed-threshold true positives degrade with greater distance, supporting the motivation to approach before rejecting.

metaexplore.title: Meta-Explore: Exploratory Hierarchical Vision-and-Language Navigation Using Scene Object Spectrum Grounding
metaexplore.problem: Recover from an incorrect high-level route by selecting a useful local destination in an online topological graph. The method starts from a DUET-style graph navigator and uses object-layout grounding to choose recovery goals.
metaexplore.method: A graph cross-modal encoder feeds navigation, object grounding, progress, and mode heads. The paper calls ordinary goal-directed navigation exploration and corrective graph traversal exploitation. Mode supervision labels detours off the shortest route; a threshold of 0.5 activates recovery. Progress predicts 1 minus current/start goal distance with squared loss. A correlation regularizer, action imitation, and object grounding accompany actor-critic fine-tuning. Scene object spectra are built from category-specific binary bounding-box masks: log magnitude of a 2-D Fourier transform is vertically averaged and normalized into a K by eta representation. An instruction-derived spectrum uses an object list and average box width. Candidate recovery destinations are scored by spectrum similarity along a corrected shortest initial-to-candidate path, and the agent physically traverses the graph shortest path to the selected frontier. No future-view image is generated by this method.
metaexplore.novelty: Adds instruction-conditioned object-spectrum recovery goals and learned switching to a DUET-based hierarchical agent. Spectrum grounding represents object arrangements beyond an unordered object bag, but magnitude spectra discard translation phase, and the instruction-to-object conversion does not preserve all relational language.

vsi_bench.title: Thinking in Space: How Multimodal Large Language Models See, Remember, and Recall Spaces
vsi_bench.problem: Evaluate spatial reasoning from indoor video, including counting, dimensions, distances, directions, route planning, and appearance order. This is offline video question answering, not an interactive navigation policy evaluation.
vsi_bench.method:
VSI-Bench derives questions from ScanNet, ScanNet++, and ARKit scene reconstructions and videos. Most questions use 3-D annotations and templates, with human route-planning annotations and iterative human filtering. Four tasks require numeric answers (object count, absolute distance, object size, room size); four use multiple-choice answers (relative distance, relative direction, route planning, appearance order). Numeric scoring averages relative-error thresholds from 0.5 through 0.95; multiple-choice scoring extracts answer letters/text. Fifteen pretrained models are evaluated zero-shot with greedy decoding. Additional controlled prompt experiments use CoT, tree-style reasoning, and five-sample self-consistency. Grid-map prompting asks models to place objects in a 10 by 10 or 20 by 20 map; supplied ground-truth maps separate perception/memory errors from map-use errors.

SUPPLEMENT CHECK: pp. 1–3 select 150 ARKitScenes, 50 ScanNet++ and 88 ScanNet videos; suppress rare/small objects and ambiguous geometry; and construct route-plan questions as filling turn directions in human-specified routes. Post-answer self-explanations are elicited after a prediction, unlike pre-answer CoT. Error attribution covers 163 selected errors with fractional assignment to overlapping categories; this is an interpretive diagnostic, not a causal intervention on internal computation. Cognitive maps use a 10 by 10 grid; all category names are supplied for map visualization, while the relative-distance intervention supplies only question-mentioned categories.
vsi_bench.novelty: Provides a video spatial reasoning benchmark and tests whether explicit language reasoning or spatial representations improve answers. The map intervention is stronger evidence about usable spatial information than an attention picture, but the generated map is an external prediction rather than direct measurement of a model’s latent world state.
vsi_bench.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 1 full benchmark Gemini-1.5-Pro 45.4 and GPT-4o 34.0, compared with a frequent-answer baseline 34.0; seven of twelve open models fall below that baseline. Human 79.2 is measured on a 400-question subset (50 per task), where Gemini scores 48.8, so human/full-set comparisons must preserve denominators. On 163 wrong subset answers, a self-explanation-based audit attributes 71% to spatial issues; this categorization is not a causal latent-mechanism test. CoT/tree prompting decreases mean performance by roughly four points in tested configurations and self-consistency by 1.1, without establishing that language reasoning always harms navigation. embodiedqa.title: Embodied Question Answering
embodiedqa.problem: An agent must move through a previously unseen House3D home to obtain visual evidence and answer a question. EQA v1 deliberately restricts questions to one target object, enabling shortest-path demonstrations. It is active visual QA, not natural-language route following.
embodiedqa.method:
EQA v1 filters SUNCG scenes and generates functional-program questions, excluding answer distributions with normalized entropy below 0.5 and questions seen in fewer than four environments. It has 4,246/506/529 train/validation/test questions in disjoint 643/67/57 homes. Four evaluated types are location, color, color-in-room, and spatial preposition. A four-block CNN is pretrained for RGB reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and depth. Separate two-layer 128-dimensional question LSTMs serve navigation and answering. PACMAN uses a recurrent planner choosing forward/left/right/stop and an MLP controller repeating an action up to five times before returning control. Actions move at most 0.25 m or turn 9 degrees. The answer head attends over only the last five frames and predicts one of 172 answers. Supervised navigation cross-entropy trains 15 epochs under a distance curriculum; QA trains 50 epochs. REINFORCE then fine-tunes the navigator with the answerer frozen, using a terminal correct-answer reward of 5 and forward-distance shaping coefficient 0.005. Evaluation starts 10, 30, or 50 actions before the goal and caps episodes at 100 actions.

SUPPLEMENT CHECK: pp. 1–2 describe functional-program question generation, uniqueness constraints and entropy/count filtering; nine generator templates do not mean nine types were used in every main experiment. Page 3 pretrains visual features with semantic segmentation, depth and reconstruction, using Adam at 1e-3, batch 20 and five epochs over 100,000 images. The QA component attends to the final five frames. Page 4 contrasts human versus shortest-path views: worse answer rank on human routes is evidence of view-distribution mismatch, not worse human navigation ability.
embodiedqa.novelty: Introduces embodied active QA and a planner/controller temporal hierarchy, combining existing CNN/RNN, imitation, and policy-gradient ingredients. The main distinction from passive VQA is control over observations; unlike IQA, object manipulation is not required.
embodiedqa.results: PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 1 at T−30, imitation PACMAN ends 1.50 m from target with QA mean rank 3.13; RL ends 2.19 m away with improved mean rank 2.99 and stops in only 32% of episodes. Authors explicitly observe overshooting. The shortest-path QA oracle has mean rank 3.21, showing the closest endpoint is not necessarily the most informative view. The question-conditioned LSTM ends at 2.23 m, supporting the hierarchy for navigation, but the small QA mean-rank changes should not be presented as high accuracy. Human navigation uses a subset and a different answer output, so there is no directly comparable human mean rank.

iqa.title: IQA: Visual Question Answering in Interactive Environments
iqa.problem: Answer existence, counting, and spatial-relation questions by navigating and opening/closing containers in AI2-THOR. The floor is discretized, localization is supplied, and objects must be visible and close enough for interaction. IQUAD has 76,800 training and 1,920 test configurations across 25 and five kitchen rooms.
iqa.method: HIMN factorizes a high-level GRU planner and low-level Navigator, Scanner, Detector, Manipulator, and Answerer. A 32-action high-level policy selects relative waypoints in a 5×5 grid, view rotations, interactions, or answer. Semantic spatial memory stores detection probabilities, occupancy, coverage, and visit intent. An egocentric spatial GRU updates only the current local window in a global tensor; other locations persist. A* replans over predicted occupancy while a supervised navigation head predicts feasibility/termination. YOLOv3 fine-tuned on training scenes and a depth network project objects into the map; scanning and manipulation controllers have fixed environment-defined behavior. The answerer convolves the full map with a tiled question vector, pools, and predicts the answer. Separate pretraining uses oracle planners/detections/partial maps where appropriate, followed by joint learning. A3C trains the planner with answer, exploration coverage, invalid-action and time rewards; an auxiliary supervised loss predicts validity of all actions.
iqa.novelty: Extends embodied QA to actions that change visibility and object state, and introduces local writes into persistent global semantic memory. Memory and control factorization are central; there is no VLM backbone or zero-training claim.
iqa.results: PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 2 HIMN with YOLO reaches 68.47% existence, 30.43% counting, 58.67% spatial accuracy versus chance 50/25/50. Episodes average 318/926/516 actions, much longer than the small human sample. Table 3 oracle detection raises existence to 86.56 and spatial to 70.94; oracle navigation further raises counting to 48.44. Removing question input to the planner or the auxiliary validity loss returns performance near chance. Thus semantics and affordance supervision both matter. Table 5 explicitly separates novel arrangements in seen rooms from five unseen rooms. §5.5 acknowledges that the 2-D map cannot distinguish inside from on top and exploration revisits are inefficient.
iqa.implementation: INSPECTED CODE: networks/qa_planner_network.py constructs question-conditioned memory crops and answer/planning heads. answer_loss:220–243 uses sigmoid cross-entropy for existence/spatial answers and softmax cross-entropy for counting; move_loss:245–252 adds a ten-weighted sigmoid loss for all possible moves when enabled. This confirms auxiliary action-validity supervision in addition to question answering and RL, not an instruction-language-only learner. The release includes TensorFlow/A3C training, supervised map/navigation training, AI2-THOR interaction, question generation and evaluation entry points. Their existence is not a claim each simulator transition was audited. No simulator, training or evaluation was executed; legacy THOR/vision-model assets are prerequisites.

embodiedgap.title: Rethinking the Embodied Gap in Vision-and-Language Navigation: A Holistic Study of Physical and Visual Disparities
embodiedgap.problem: VLN-CE movement abstractions omit locomotion, falls, controller effects, camera differences, and lighting. VLN-PE evaluates ego-centric agents in physically simulated humanoid, quadruped, and wheeled embodiments using GRUtopia/Isaac Sim.
embodiedgap.method:
Ninety MP3D scenes are converted to USD and mesh holes manually repaired. Stairs are removed because controllers cannot reliably negotiate them, leaving 8,679/658/1,347 R2R train/seen/unseen episodes. Ten synthetic GRScenes and one Gaussian-splat laboratory add rendering/domain conditions. Baselines include Seq2Seq, CMA, NaVid, an adapted VLMaps with frontier exploration, and the new RDP. RDP encodes RGB/text with LongCLIP and depth with ResNet-50, uses cross-modal attention and GRU memory, and predicts eight relative (delta x, delta y, delta yaw) actions with a Transformer DDPM head. Noise-prediction MSE plus stop-progress MSE weighted 10 trains it. A separate stop head is necessary because diffusion actions do not reliably imply stopping. Metrics add fall and stuck rates to navigation success/path efficiency; the map-based comparison uses only 200 sampled episodes.

SUPPLEMENT CHECK: Appendix A supplies the RDP details: LongCLIP RGB/text features plus depth and a point goal, five RGB tokens of width 512, GRU history, four previous actions and relative coordinates. Diffusion predicts eight future actions and executes four; a heuristic stops when action magnitudes are below 0.1 or progress exceeds 0.8. Training is reported as about two days on four RTX 4090s, batch eight and lr 1e-4. Fall/stuck definitions and controller choices are operational benchmark components, not abstract navigation correctness.
embodiedgap.novelty: Primarily a platform and controlled transfer study, plus a recurrent diffusion-action baseline. Its physical simulation is more realistic than graph navigation or idealized CE, but does not itself prove real-robot reliability. Data collected with different controllers and embodiments test concrete sources of transfer error.
embodiedgap.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 1 NaVid zero-shot H1 unseen SR/SPL 22.42/18.58; RDP trained in VLN-PE 21.98/16.44; fine-tuned CMA 23.31/19.66. These compare different data/parameter budgets. Table 4 controller-consistent CMA training/evaluation gives 18.78 SR versus 13.51 when trained without locomotion but tested with it; falls remain 18.63%. Table 5 adding all embodiments and CE data raises H1 SR 18.78→26.87 but confounds diversity and data amount. Table 6 NaVid SR falls 22.42→9.95 under dim light, while RGB-D RDP is stable near 22%; modality differs. Authors report NaVid rotating over 25 steps near goals in 70% of episodes. Gaussian-lab NaVid SR 5.81 is an observed failure, while rendering-noise attribution is their hypothesis. The study exposes concrete embodiment/stopping fragility while excluding stairs.

SUPPLEMENT CHECK: Appendix C, p. 4, reports a 14-episode Unitree Go2 CMA test improving SR from 7.14% to 28.57%, with a custom STOP probability threshold above 1e-4 because the transferred policy did not stop robustly. This small physical test is not real-world validation of RDP. Evaluation is restricted to egocentric methods, and the Jetbot camera is raised in simulation (Fig. 14). walkreadless.title: Walk and Read Less: Improving the Efficiency of Vision-and-Language Navigation via Tuning-Free Multimodal Token Pruning
walkreadless.problem: Removing visual/text tokens can lower per-step compute while increasing navigation length and removing critical action options. NAP changes inference of existing trained HAMT, DUET, and GOAT agents without additional parameter tuning.
walkreadless.method: Background pruning retains all navigable action-view tokens and removes low column-summed attention background tokens at each visual layer. Backtracking pruning retains only top-scored unvisited graph frontier nodes from earlier steps, reducing both graph tokens and available recovery destinations. Vocabulary priority pruning first builds an offline training-lexicon dictionary using Llama 3 relevance judgments; at each language layer it preferentially removes dictionary-irrelevant tokens, with attention ranking filling or reducing the pruning quota. The LLM is not called during navigation. The cost metric sums instruction encoder FLOPs once and visual/cross-modal FLOPs over decision steps using thop. CE uses ETPNav and its waypoint predictor. No new loss or fine-tuning is required, but the base policy, feature encoders and waypoint predictor are pretrained.
walkreadless.novelty: Task-specific foreground protection and graph-action pruning improve the accuracy/compute frontier relative to generic token pruning. The vocabulary is a context-independent relevance heuristic, not instruction entailment or semantic-preservation certification.
walkreadless.results: PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 2 GOAT at roughly 50% tokens has R2R SR 73.8 versus full 78.1 and FLOPs 55.6%; RxR 63.9 versus 69.6 and FLOPs 49.3%; REVERIE 49.6 versus 53.8 and FLOPs 48.3%. The gain is over other pruned baselines, not full-model accuracy. Table 3 RxR SPL 61.8→54.3, steps 8.2→9.0. CE Table 7 full 56.9 SR/8.8 steps→52.7/9.6 with FLOPs 62.4%; pruning does not always shorten motion. Appendix F Table 13 calls one and flight irrelevant in a stair instruction: this is a documented prompt output and an untested numerical-language risk, not measured failure frequency. FLOPs do not establish wall-clock latency on target hardware. Appendix Table 11 has different step counts from main Table 2, limiting direct cross-table interpretation.

BTP removes the earliest encountered unvisited nodes beyond its threshold from model input (agent.py:134–184). BGP normally preserves action-candidate features and ranks only background features; its action_included ablation can prune actions (models/pruning/bgp.py:107–206). VPP prioritizes tokens using a context-free irrelevant-token ID set, then restores the surviving tokens’ original order (models/pruning/vpp.py:1–99). These are tuning-free operations on an already trained navigator, not an untrained model. The main entry point runs evaluation and computes environment metrics.
